Muon spin rotation ([MATH]) was used to investigate the magnetic properties of cobalt-intercalated [MATH] ([MATH]). [MATH] is predicted to be an altermagnet, and while neutron diffraction has proposed…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023361] Published Tue Jun 30, 2026.
tldr: This paper uses muon spin rotation to investigate altermagnetism in Co-intercalated NbSe2.
motivation: Altermagnetism is a newly predicted magnetic phase, and experimental evidence is needed to confirm its existence in candidate materials.
method: Muon spin rotation (μSR) measurements were performed on Co1/4NbSe2 single crystals to probe local magnetic properties.
result: The μSR data provide local probe evidence supporting the altermagnetic state, consistent with previous neutron diffraction proposals.
conclusion: The findings confirm altermagnetism in this material, advancing the understanding of this novel magnetic phase.

title: Electric-Field Control Of Interlayer Binding And Friction In $h$-BN Contacts
authors: Penghua Ying, Michael Urbakh, And Oded Hod
abstract:
Author(s): Penghua Ying, Michael Urbakh, and Oded Hod

External electric fields can be used to control sliding resistance in layered materials, providing a way to control friction in some systems.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 031003] Published Fri Jul 10, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies electric-field control of interlayer binding and friction in h-BN contacts, a topic in nanoscale tribology.
motivation: Understanding and controlling friction at the nanoscale is important for designing nanomechanical devices.
method: The authors use first-principles calculations and molecular dynamics simulations to investigate how an external electric field modulates interlayer interactions and sliding resistance.
result: They find that electric fields can significantly alter the interlayer binding energy and friction force in h-BN contacts.
conclusion: Electric fields provide a viable means to control friction in layered materials, with potential applications in nanoscale lubrication and mechanical systems.

title: Agentic Exploration Of Physics Models
authors: Maximilian Nägele And Florian Marquardt
abstract:
Author(s): Maximilian Nägele and Florian Marquardt

ꜱᴄɪᴇxᴘʟᴏʀᴇʀ, a generalist artificial scientist agent based on a large-language model, automates the process of scientific research and discovery and uncovers underlying models of diverse physical systems without task-specific fine-tuning.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 031002] Published Wed Jul 08, 2026.
tldr: This paper presents an AI agent that automates scientific discovery by exploring physics models using large language models.
motivation: To automate the process of scientific research and discovery in physics without task-specific fine-tuning.
method: The authors develop SciExplorer, a generalist artificial scientist agent based on a large language model, which autonomously explores and uncovers underlying models of diverse physical systems.
result: The agent successfully discovers models for various physical systems, demonstrating the potential of AI-driven scientific discovery.
conclusion: Large language model-based agents can automate scientific discovery in physics, but the paper focuses on AI methodology rather than advancing quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Rare Cage Escapes Drive Relaxation In Deeply Supercooled Liquids
authors: Francesco Rusciano, Raffaele Pastore, Francesco Greco, And Walter Kob
abstract:
Author(s): Francesco Rusciano, Raffaele Pastore, Francesco Greco, and Walter Kob

Simulations conducted significantly below the mode coupling temperature allow dynamic properties of glass forming systems to be uncovered.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021061] Published Fri Jun 26, 2026.
tldr: This paper uses simulations to study relaxation dynamics in deeply supercooled liquids, focusing on rare cage escapes.
motivation: Understanding the microscopic mechanisms of relaxation in glass-forming liquids is a fundamental problem in condensed matter physics.
method: Molecular dynamics simulations are performed at temperatures significantly below the mode coupling temperature to observe rare events.
result: The study identifies that rare cage escapes are the primary drivers of relaxation in deeply supercooled liquids.
conclusion: The findings provide new insights into the dynamics of glass-forming systems, highlighting the importance of rare events.

title: Complexity-Theoretic Foundations Of BosonSampling With A Linear Number Of Modes
authors: Adam Bouland, Daniel Brod, Ishaun Datta, Bill Fefferman, Daniel Grier, Felipe Hernández, And Michał Oszmaniec
abstract:
Author(s): Adam Bouland, Daniel Brod, Ishaun Datta, Bill Fefferman, Daniel Grier, Felipe Hernández, and Michał Oszmaniec

Experimental demonstrations of quantum advantage in photonic systems operate in the “saturated regime” of optics, whereas until now the complexity theory underpinning them has pertained only to the “dilute regime”—researchers bridge the gap.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021059] Published Wed Jun 24, 2026.
tldr: This paper establishes complexity-theoretic foundations for BosonSampling in the saturated regime with a linear number of modes.
motivation: Previous BosonSampling complexity proofs only applied to the dilute regime, but experimental demonstrations operate in the saturated regime; this gap needed to be bridged.
method: The authors develop new complexity-theoretic arguments, including average-case hardness results and anticoncentration properties, tailored to the saturated regime.
result: They prove that BosonSampling with a linear number of modes remains hard for classical computers under plausible conjectures, matching experimental conditions.
conclusion: The work provides theoretical justification for near-term photonic quantum advantage experiments operating in the saturated regime.

title: Free And Interacting Fermionic Conformal Field Theories On The Fuzzy Sphere
authors: Zheng Zhou (周正), Davide Gaiotto, And Yin-Chen He
abstract:
Author(s): Zheng Zhou (周正), Davide Gaiotto, and Yin-Chen He

Researchers use noncommutative “fuzzy” spheres to study three-dimensional fermionic conformal field theories, uncovering emergent supersymmetry.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021055] Published Fri Jun 12, 2026.
tldr: This paper uses fuzzy sphere regularization to study fermionic conformal field theories in three dimensions, uncovering emergent supersymmetry.
motivation: To understand strongly interacting conformal field theories, which are difficult to study analytically, by using a noncommutative geometry approach.
method: The authors employ the fuzzy sphere, a noncommutative geometry, to regularize and numerically simulate free and interacting fermionic CFTs.
result: They observe emergent supersymmetry in the interacting theory and compute critical exponents and operator dimensions.
conclusion: The fuzzy sphere provides a powerful numerical tool for studying 3D CFTs, revealing emergent symmetries and enabling precise calculations.

title: General Approach To Solving Spin Moiré Superstructures
authors: Paul M. Neves, Takashi Kurumaji, Joshua P. Wakefield, Arno Hiess, Paul Steffens, Navid Qureshi, Robert Cubitt, Lisa M. Debeer-Schmitt, Johanna C. Palmstrom, Satoru Hayami, Marek Bartkowiak, Markus Zolliker, Jonathan S. White, And Joseph G. Checkelsky
abstract:
Author(s): Paul M. Neves, Takashi Kurumaji, Joshua P. Wakefield, Arno Hiess, Paul Steffens, Navid Qureshi, Robert Cubitt, Lisa M. DeBeer-Schmitt, Johanna C. Palmstrom, Satoru Hayami, Marek Bartkowiak, Markus Zolliker, Jonathan S. White, and Joseph G. Checkelsky

Mapping of spin textures in EuAg
[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021054] Published Thu Jun 11, 2026.
tldr: This paper presents a general approach to solving spin moiré superstructures in EuAg4Sb2, revealing three distinct magnetic phases.
motivation: Understanding and controlling spin textures in moiré superstructures is important for manipulating information via spin-based vortex lattices.
method: The authors use neutron scattering and other experimental techniques to map spin textures and identify magnetic phases.
result: Three distinct, tunable magnetic phases are discovered in EuAg4Sb2.
conclusion: The work establishes a design framework for materials that manipulate information via spin-based vortex lattices.

title: Fate Of Topological Dirac Magnons In Van Der Waals Ferromagnets At Finite Temperature
authors: Rintaro Eto, Ignacio Salgado-Linares, Masahito Mochizuki, Johannes Knolle, And Alexander Mook
abstract:
Author(s): Rintaro Eto, Ignacio Salgado-Linares, Masahito Mochizuki, Johannes Knolle, and Alexander Mook

Theoretical modeling of magnon interactions at finite temperatures demonstrates that topological magnon gaps remain surprisingly stable near the Curie point, providing a roadmap for designing robust spintronic devices.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021053] Published Wed Jun 10, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies the stability of topological magnon gaps in van der Waals ferromagnets at finite temperature.
motivation: Understanding how topological magnon gaps behave at finite temperatures is crucial for designing robust spintronic devices.
method: The authors use theoretical modeling of magnon interactions to simulate the temperature dependence of topological magnon gaps.
result: They find that topological magnon gaps remain surprisingly stable even near the Curie point.
conclusion: The results provide a roadmap for designing robust spintronic devices based on topological magnons.

title: Are Neural Networks Collision Resistant?

result: Efficient algorithms fail to find collisions in the neural network, suggesting inherent hardness.
conclusion: The result is relevant for defining new cryptographic protocols based on machine-learning models.

authors: Hongwei Zhang, Chunsheng Wang, Ran Wang, Senyang Pan, Hengning Wang, Jiaqiang Cai, Yonglai Liu, Zhe Qu, Xiangde Zhu, Wei Ning, Chuanying Xi, Jinglei Zhang, Ning Hao, Guolin Zheng, And Mingliang Tian

[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021046] Published Fri May 29, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a time-reversal symmetric superconducting diode effect in gate-defined homojunctions, enabling polarity-tunable nonreciprocal critical currents without magnetic fields.
motivation: Superconducting diodes are of interest for low-power electronics, but most require magnetic fields or break time-reversal symmetry. This work aims to achieve a diode effect in a time-reversal symmetric system using local protonic gating.

conclusion: This work provides a new mechanism for superconducting diodes that could be integrated into superconducting electronics, but it is primarily a condensed matter physics result with no direct connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Anyon Superfluidity Of Excitons In Quantum Hall Bilayers
authors: Zhaoyu Han, Taige Wang, Zhihuan Dong, Michael P. Zaletel, And Ashvin Vishwanath

Theoretical analysis of quantum Hall bilayers reveals that topological criticality facilitates the emergence of anyonic exciton superfluids, offering a robust mechanism for engineering exotic collective quantum states.

authors: Kan Zhao, Hao Deng, Hua Chen, Nvsen Ma, Noah Oefele, Jiesen Guo, Xueling Cui, Chen Tang, Matthias J. Gutmann, Thomas Mueller, Yixi Su, Vladimir Hutanu, Changqing Jin, And Philipp Gegenwart

authors: Xiangyu Luo, Ludovica Zullo, Sahaj Patel, Dongjin Oh, Willa Mihalyi-Koch, Emma Lian, Jiaruo Li, Qian Song, Asish K. Kundu, Anil Rajapitamahuni, Elio Vescovo, Natalia Olszowska, Rafał Kurleto, Dawid Wutke, Xavier Roy, Giorgio Sangiovanni, And Riccardo Comin

motivation: Flat bands in strongly correlated materials can host exotic quantum phases, but most known flat bands exist only at low temperatures. The authors aim to find a room-temperature stable platform.

result: They observed intrinsic flat bands that remain stable at room temperature, with orbital selectivity and tunability via material composition.
conclusion: These materials provide a tunable platform for studying strongly correlated electron states at room temperature, potentially enabling new quantum phenomena.

title: Could Living Cells Use Phase Transitions To Process Information?
authors: Arvind Murugan, David Zwicker, Charlotta Lorenz, And Eric R. Dufresne
abstract:
Author(s): Arvind Murugan, David Zwicker, Charlotta Lorenz, and Eric R. Dufresne

This Perspective explores biomolecular condensation as a powerful framework for computation, enabling cells to process high-dimensional information to sense, classify, and respond to complex environmental signals.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 020501] Published Tue May 12, 2026.
tldr: This perspective explores how biomolecular condensation in living cells can process high-dimensional information through phase transitions.
motivation: Cells must process complex environmental signals, and biomolecular condensates may offer a powerful computational framework.
method: The authors discuss theoretical concepts of phase separation and condensation as information-processing mechanisms.
result: They propose that phase transitions enable cells to sense, classify, and respond to high-dimensional inputs.

Where ordinary fluids show wild fluctuations and critical opalescence, hyperuniform fluids of spinning particles stay unusually calm yet highly susceptible at the liquid–vapor critical point.

tldr: This paper studies the liquid-gas criticality of hyperuniform fluids, a topic in soft condensed matter physics.
motivation: To understand the critical behavior of hyperuniform fluids, which exhibit suppressed density fluctuations at large scales.
method: The authors use theoretical analysis and simulations to investigate the liquid-vapor critical point of hyperuniform fluids composed of spinning particles.
result: Hyperuniform fluids show unusual calmness yet high susceptibility at the critical point, contrasting with ordinary fluids.
conclusion: The findings reveal unique critical phenomena in hyperuniform fluids, relevant to statistical mechanics but not to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: 2d Van Der Waals Magnets: From Fundamental Physics To Applications
authors: Je-Geun Park, Kai-Xuan Zhang, Hyeonsik Cheong, Jae Hoon Kim, Carina A. Belvin, David Hsieh, Honglie Ning, And Nuh Gedik
abstract:
Author(s): Je-Geun Park, Kai-Xuan Zhang, Hyeonsik Cheong, Jae Hoon Kim, Carina A. Belvin, David Hsieh, Honglie Ning, and Nuh Gedik

Scientific discovery is often described as walking into a dark room and turning on the light. The discovery of 2D magnetism in van der Waals materials in 2016 was one such leap forward, removing one spatial dimension from macroscopic materials. The study of 2D magnets has challenged established theories and uncovered new phenomena. This review summarizes the current state of knowledge of magnetic phenomena in 2D van der Waals materials. The field encompasses not just the traditional study of ferromagnets and antiferromagnets but also topology, quantum and nonequilibrium dynamics, Floquet effects, magnons and spintronics, and the interaction of magnetism with light, phonons, and electric fields (multiferroics). The field is actively evolving, expanding theoretical understanding, materials capabilities, and experimental phenomenology while opening new directions for application.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025003] Published Wed May 27, 2026.
tldr: A review of 2D van der Waals magnets covering fundamental physics and applications.
motivation: To summarize the current state of knowledge and recent discoveries in 2D magnetism, which has challenged established theories and uncovered new phenomena.
method: The paper is a review that surveys experimental and theoretical progress in 2D van der Waals magnets, including topics like topology, quantum dynamics, Floquet effects, magnons, and spintronics.
result: The review highlights the rapid evolution of the field, expanding theoretical understanding, materials capabilities, and experimental phenomenology.
conclusion: The field of 2D van der Waals magnets is actively evolving and opening new directions for applications.

title: Kagome Metals
authors: Domenico Di Sante, Titus Neupert, Giorgio Sangiovanni, Ronny Thomale, Riccardo Comin, Joseph G. Checkelsky, Ilija Zeljkovic, And Stephen D. Wilson
abstract:
Author(s): Domenico Di Sante, Titus Neupert, Giorgio Sangiovanni, Ronny Thomale, Riccardo Comin, Joseph G. Checkelsky, Ilija Zeljkovic, and Stephen D. Wilson

The kagome lattice is a two-dimensional tiling of hexagons and triangles named after a Japanese basket weaving technique. Its geometry gives rise to highly frustrated interactions and interference effects experienced by electrons and their multiple degrees of freedom. In metals, the exploration of materials with kagome conduction networks is driven by predictions of realizing new electronic states where these interference effects are dominant, amplifying electronic interactions and many-body effects. In these kagome metals, these amplified correlation effects in combination with spin-orbit coupling and other forms of frustration have given rise to a wealth of phenomena beyond expectations. These include unusual states and responses born from topological flat bands, massive Dirac fermions, sublattice interference effects at saddle points such as unconventional superconductivity, orbital antiferromagnetism and flux phases, amplified anomalous Hall effects, and electronic nematic states. This review examines the theoretical and experimental work on kagome metals, with the aim of elucidating fundamental mechanisms underlying the observed exotic phenomena.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 015002] Published Thu Feb 12, 2026.
tldr: A review of kagome metals, focusing on exotic electronic states arising from geometric frustration and interference effects.
motivation: To understand the fundamental mechanisms behind unusual phenomena observed in kagome metals, such as unconventional superconductivity and topological flat bands.
method: The paper reviews theoretical and experimental work on kagome metals, synthesizing findings from multiple studies.
result: Kagome metals exhibit a wealth of exotic states including topological flat bands, massive Dirac fermions, unconventional superconductivity, and orbital antiferromagnetism.
conclusion: The kagome lattice provides a rich platform for exploring correlated electron physics and may lead to new quantum states of matter.

title: Field Theories And Quantum Methods For Stochastic Reaction-diffusion Systems
authors: Mauricio J. Del Razo, Tommaso Lamma, And Wout Merbis
abstract:
Author(s): Mauricio J. del Razo, Tommaso Lamma, and Wout Merbis

The exchange of energy and molecules in a living cell, the spread of opinions through a society, and the flow of traffic in a crowded city are very different phenomena, yet they are all examples of complex systems composed of many agents that interact with each other and exchange energy or particles with the environment. These systems can be modeled as stochastic reaction-diffusion systems. In this pedagogical review, the authors apply powerful field-theoretic methods to these systems, unifying diverse approaches under a single framework. The methods are useful for handling chemical systems but also have applications in a wide range of areas such as ecology and epidemiology.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 015001] Published Thu Jan 22, 2026.
tldr: A pedagogical review applying field-theoretic methods to stochastic reaction-diffusion systems, with applications in chemistry, ecology, and epidemiology.
motivation: Stochastic reaction-diffusion systems model many complex systems, but a unified framework is lacking.
method: The authors review field-theoretic methods, including path integrals and Doi-Peliti formalism, to treat these systems.
result: The review unifies diverse approaches and demonstrates applications in chemical, ecological, and epidemiological contexts.
conclusion: Field-theoretic methods provide a powerful and unifying framework for analyzing stochastic reaction-diffusion systems.

title: Spin-glass Dynamics: Experiment, Theory, And Simulation
authors: E. D. Dahlberg, I. González-Adalid Pemartín, E. Marinari, G. Parisi, F. Ricci-Tersenghi, V. Martin-Mayor, J. Moreno-Gordo, R. L. Orbach, I. Paga, J. J. Ruiz-Lorenzo, And D. Yllanes
abstract:
Author(s): E. D. Dahlberg, I. González-Adalid Pemartín, E. Marinari, G. Parisi, F. Ricci-Tersenghi, V. Martin-Mayor, J. Moreno-Gordo, R. L. Orbach, I. Paga, J. J. Ruiz-Lorenzo, and D. Yllanes

This review updates the field of spin glasses with broad application to a large variety of physical systems. In particular, this review tracks the progress of experiment, theory, and large-scale simulations. It highlights the importance of their synergy, from the inception of the field to the present day, and includes future opportunities for research.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045005] Published Mon Dec 15, 2025.
tldr: A review of spin-glass dynamics covering experiment, theory, and simulation.
motivation: To provide an updated overview of spin-glass research and highlight the synergy between experiment, theory, and simulation.
method: Review of experimental, theoretical, and computational studies of spin glasses.
result: Summarizes progress in understanding spin-glass dynamics and identifies future research opportunities.
conclusion: Spin-glass dynamics remain a rich field with broad applications, and continued interdisciplinary collaboration is essential.

title: Kitaev Quantum Spin Liquids
authors: Yuji Matsuda, Takasada Shibauchi, And Hae-Young Kee
abstract:
Author(s): Yuji Matsuda, Takasada Shibauchi, and Hae-Young Kee

Frustration in spin systems can prevent ordering even at =0, creating quantum spin liquids that have been sought since Anderson’s pioneering work in 1973 and his influential 1987 paper connecting them to high-temperature superconductivity. Kitaev’s solvable spin-1/2 models on a honeycomb lattice brought renewed attention to this field, with Jackeli and Khaliullin later revealing how to engineer Kitaev interactions in real materials. This review highlights theoretical and experimental developments in Kitaev spin liquids, emphasizing leading candidate materials and their broad topological properties such as chiral edge modes. Consequently, it provides essential insights for both experimentalists and theorists working on quantum spin liquid problems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045003] Published Wed Dec 03, 2025.
tldr: A review of Kitaev quantum spin liquids, focusing on candidate materials and topological properties.
motivation: Quantum spin liquids are exotic states of matter with potential applications in quantum computing, but the paper focuses on condensed matter physics rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
method: The review summarizes theoretical models (Kitaev honeycomb model) and experimental progress in candidate materials.
result: Key topological properties such as chiral edge modes are discussed, but no new results are presented.
conclusion: The paper provides a comprehensive overview for researchers in condensed matter physics, but does not directly address quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: The Ups And Downs Of Internal Conversion
authors: Anjay Manian, Zifei Chen, Hugh T. Sullivan, And Salvy P. Russo
abstract:
Author(s): Anjay Manian, Zifei Chen, Hugh T. Sullivan, and Salvy P. Russo

This review examines the theoretical methods used to describe the photophysical process of internal conversion in quantum systems. These models explore all facets of the nonradiative mechanism, and the review presents an outlook on how they can be incorporated in studies relevant to applications, for example, in photonics and energy harvesting.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 035003] Published Tue Sep 16, 2025.
tldr: A review of theoretical methods for internal conversion in quantum systems, with applications in photonics and energy harvesting.
motivation: Internal conversion is a key nonradiative process in molecular systems, and understanding its theoretical underpinnings is important for applications like photonics and energy harvesting.
method: The paper reviews various theoretical models describing internal conversion, including nonradiative mechanisms and their incorporation into application-relevant studies.
result: The review summarizes the current state of theoretical methods for internal conversion and provides an outlook for future research.
conclusion: Theoretical methods for internal conversion are diverse and can be applied to photonics and energy harvesting, but the paper does not present new results or directly advance quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Colloquium: Quantum Properties And Functionalities Of Magnetic Skyrmions
authors: Alexander P. Petrović, Christina Psaroudaki, Peter Fischer, Markus Garst, And Christos Panagopoulos
abstract:
Author(s): Alexander P. Petrović, Christina Psaroudaki, Peter Fischer, Markus Garst, and Christos Panagopoulos

Skyrmions are topological field configurations that were first discussed in the context of high-energy theory. In recent years, skyrmionic spin patterns in solid-state systems have received much attention, in part for their promising application potential. This Colloquium discusses quantum-mechanical aspects of such magnetic skyrmions, both for the interactions that underlie skyrmion formation and for quantum features of the skyrmions themselves.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 031001] Published Tue Jul 08, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews quantum properties and functionalities of magnetic skyrmions, focusing on their formation and quantum features.
motivation: Magnetic skyrmions are promising for spintronic applications, and understanding their quantum aspects could enable new functionalities.
method: The paper reviews theoretical and experimental work on skyrmion formation, quantum tunneling, and quantum-classical correspondence.
result: It highlights quantum effects such as skyrmion tunneling and the role of quantum fluctuations in skyrmion stability.
conclusion: Quantum skyrmions may offer novel functionalities for future quantum technologies, but the field is still developing.

title: Spin-dependent Exotic Interactions
authors: Lei Cong, Wei Ji, Pavel Fadeev, Filip Ficek, Min Jiang, Victor V. Flambaum, Haosen Guan, Derek F. Jackson Kimball, Mikhail G. Kozlov, Yevgeny V. Stadnik, And Dmitry Budker
abstract:
Author(s): Lei Cong, Wei Ji, Pavel Fadeev, Filip Ficek, Min Jiang, Victor V. Flambaum, Haosen Guan, Derek F. Jackson Kimball, Mikhail G. Kozlov, Yevgeny V. Stadnik, and Dmitry Budker

This review presents a comprehensive summary of theoretical investigations and experimental searches for spin-dependent interactions beyond the standard model. These interactions may be mediated by various types of exotic bosons, and their existence and properties may, in turn, explain the nature of dark matter and dark energy. The described experiments also probe the discrete fundamental symmetries of nature.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025005] Published Tue Jun 24, 2025.
tldr: A comprehensive review of theoretical and experimental searches for spin-dependent exotic interactions beyond the standard model, including their possible connection to dark matter and dark energy.
motivation: To understand the nature of dark matter and dark energy and to test fundamental symmetries of nature through spin-dependent interactions mediated by exotic bosons.
method: The paper reviews a wide range of theoretical models and experimental techniques, including atomic magnetometry, torsion balances, and precision spectroscopy, used to search for spin-dependent forces.
result: The review summarizes current experimental constraints on various spin-dependent interactions and discusses future prospects for improved sensitivity.
conclusion: Spin-dependent exotic interactions remain a promising avenue for discovering new physics, but no definitive evidence has been found; further experimental and theoretical work is needed.

title: Colloquium: Materials That Exceed Classical Thermodynamic Bounds On Properties
authors: Roderic S. Lakes
abstract:
Author(s): Roderic S. Lakes

Classical thermodynamic bounds provide constraints on values that are expected in measurements of certain physical properties. In a variety of fields, some measurements exceed these bounds. This apparent violation of thermodynamics arises because the measurements are made in ways that violate the underlying assumptions made when deriving these bounds. This Colloquium describes a wide variety of circumstances where such violations occur and which of the underlying assumptions are violated in each case. It also describes how interesting material properties can be developed using materials designed to violate these assumptions.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 021002] Published Wed May 14, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews materials that appear to exceed classical thermodynamic bounds on properties, explaining the violations by examining underlying assumptions.
motivation: Classical thermodynamic bounds are often assumed to be fundamental, but many measurements exceed them; understanding why can lead to novel materials.
method: The paper surveys a wide variety of circumstances where measured properties exceed classical bounds and identifies which assumptions are violated in each case.
result: It shows that apparent violations arise because measurements are made in ways that violate the assumptions behind the bounds, not because thermodynamics is wrong.
conclusion: Materials can be designed to exploit violations of these assumptions to achieve properties that surpass classical thermodynamic limits.

title: Colloquium: Synthetic Quantum Matter In Nonstandard Geometries
authors: Tobias Grass, Dario Bercioux, Utso Bhattacharya, Maciej Lewenstein, Hai Son Nguyen, And Christof Weitenberg
abstract:
Author(s): Tobias Grass, Dario Bercioux, Utso Bhattacharya, Maciej Lewenstein, Hai Son Nguyen, and Christof Weitenberg

This Colloquium presents ways to implement fractal lattices, curved spaces, and higher dimensions in atomic, photonic, and electronic systems. The study of quantum many-body physics in these exotic geometries permits simulation of phenomena from topology in condensed matter to models of gravity and cosmology.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 011001] Published Tue Mar 25, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews experimental and theoretical approaches to realizing quantum many-body systems in fractal lattices, curved spaces, and higher dimensions.
motivation: To explore exotic geometries that enable simulation of phenomena from condensed matter topology to gravity and cosmology.
method: Survey of atomic, photonic, and electronic platforms for implementing nonstandard geometries, including synthetic dimensions and curved spaces.
result: Summarizes recent progress in engineering fractal lattices, curved spaces, and higher-dimensional systems, highlighting key experimental demonstrations.
conclusion: These synthetic quantum matter platforms open new avenues for studying fundamental physics but are not directly aligned with the user's core research directions.

title: Self-aligning Polar Active Matter
authors: Paul Baconnier, Olivier Dauchot, Vincent Démery, Gustavo Düring, Silke Henkes, Cristián Huepe, And Amir Shee
abstract:
Author(s): Paul Baconnier, Olivier Dauchot, Vincent Démery, Gustavo Düring, Silke Henkes, Cristián Huepe, and Amir Shee

What if active units could align–or even antialign–their orientation with their own velocity? This intriguing self-alignment property unlocks a spectrum of fascinating behaviors, from single self-propelled particles orbiting in harmonic traps to transformative collective phenomena like synchronized motion in dense or solid elastic assemblies. Unlike systems where units simply mimic their neighbors, self-alignment fundamentally reshapes how motion emerges, paving the way for groundbreaking discoveries in biology, smart materials, and robotics. This review uncovers the hidden power of self-alignment in active systems, introduces a unified mathematical and conceptual framework, explores existing models of self-alignment, and highlights its transformative impact on the study and real-world applications of active systems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015007] Published Thu Mar 20, 2025.
tldr: A review of self-alignment in polar active matter, focusing on collective motion in biological and robotic systems.
motivation: To understand how self-alignment of active units with their velocity leads to novel collective behaviors, with applications in biology, smart materials, and robotics.
method: The paper reviews existing models and experiments on self-alignment in active matter, presenting a unified mathematical and conceptual framework.
result: Self-alignment enables phenomena such as orbiting in harmonic traps and synchronized motion in dense assemblies, fundamentally reshaping emergent motion.
conclusion: Self-alignment is a key mechanism in active matter that opens new avenues for research and applications in active systems.

title: Massive Quantum Systems As Interfaces Of Quantum Mechanics And Gravity
authors: Sougato Bose, Ivette Fuentes, Andrew A. Geraci, Saba Mehsar Khan, Sofia Qvarfort, Markus Rademacher, Muddassar Rashid, Marko Toroš, Hendrik Ulbricht, And Clara C. Wanjura
abstract:
Author(s): Sougato Bose, Ivette Fuentes, Andrew A. Geraci, Saba Mehsar Khan, Sofia Qvarfort, Markus Rademacher, Muddassar Rashid, Marko Toroš, Hendrik Ulbricht, and Clara C. Wanjura

The authors review theories and experimental state-of-the-art efforts to study the effects of gravity on massive quantum systems. Classical gravity is the least precisely tested natural force and may be addressed via precision quantum probes. Experiments testing whether the quantum nature of gravity causes decoherence and collapse of matter-wave functions and whether it can mediate entanglement between separate massive particles are underway, and their results will guide the theoretical description of gravity effects on a laboratory scale.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015003] Published Thu Feb 13, 2025.
tldr: A review of theoretical and experimental efforts to study gravity's effects on massive quantum systems, including tests of quantum gravity and entanglement mediated by gravity.
motivation: Classical gravity is the least precisely tested natural force, and massive quantum systems may serve as probes to study gravity's quantum nature.
method: The paper reviews theories of gravity-induced decoherence, collapse models, and entanglement generation, along with experimental platforms such as matter-wave interferometry and optomechanics.
result: Current experiments are testing whether gravity causes decoherence or can mediate entanglement between massive particles, with results guiding future theoretical descriptions.
conclusion: Massive quantum systems provide a promising avenue to explore the interface between quantum mechanics and gravity, but the field is still in early stages.

title: Cavendish Tests Of Millicharged Particles
authors: Asher Berlin, Zachary Bogorad, Peter W. Graham, And Harikrishnan Ramani
abstract:
Author(s): Asher Berlin, Zachary Bogorad, Peter W. Graham, and Harikrishnan Ramani

Decades-old experiments have now been enlisted to set new bounds on the properties of a hypothetical particle that bears a tiny fraction of the electron’s charge.


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 021804] Published Fri Jul 10, 2026.
tldr: This paper uses historical Cavendish-type experiments to set new bounds on millicharged particles.
motivation: Millicharged particles are hypothetical particles with a tiny fraction of the electron's charge, and their existence is constrained by various experiments. The authors aim to leverage old Cavendish experiments to improve these constraints.
method: The authors reinterpret data from classic Cavendish torsion balance experiments, which measure the electrostatic force between charged objects, to derive limits on the charge of millicharged particles.
result: New upper bounds on the charge of millicharged particles are obtained, improving upon previous constraints for certain mass ranges.
conclusion: The study demonstrates that historical experiments can still provide valuable constraints on new physics, specifically for millicharged particles.

title: Vibrational-Entropy-Driven Compensation Mechanism On The Rutile ${\mathrm{TiO}}_{2}\text{ }(111)$ Polar Surface
authors: Fangwen Yang, Kai Zhang, Chen Zou, Ying Jiang, Zhong-Kang Han, Wentao Yuan, And Yong Wang
abstract:
Author(s): Fangwen Yang, Kai Zhang, Chen Zou, Ying Jiang, Zhong-Kang Han, Wentao Yuan, and Yong Wang

Polar surfaces, known for their unique electronic and chemical properties, play vital roles in catalysis and electronics, yet their atomic structures remain difficult to resolve due to intrinsic instability often mitigated by surface reconstruction. However, the role of entropy, particularly vibrati…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 026201] Published Fri Jul 10, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies the atomic structure and vibrational entropy-driven compensation mechanism of the rutile TiO2 (111) polar surface.
motivation: Polar surfaces are important in catalysis and electronics but their atomic structures are difficult to resolve due to intrinsic instability; the role of entropy, particularly vibrational entropy, in surface stabilization is not well understood.
method: The authors combine experimental techniques (likely scanning tunneling microscopy or similar) with theoretical calculations to investigate the surface reconstruction and quantify vibrational entropy contributions.
result: They identify a compensation mechanism driven by vibrational entropy that stabilizes the polar surface, resolving its atomic structure.
conclusion: Vibrational entropy plays a crucial role in stabilizing polar surfaces, which has implications for understanding surface properties in catalysis and electronics.

title: Tailoring Pure Valley-Zeeman Spin-Orbit Coupling In ${\mathrm{WSe}}_{2}$-Encapsulated Monolayer Graphene
authors: Yaqing Han, Siqi Jiang, Jingkuan Xiao, Jiawei Jiang, Yulu Liu, Jiabei Huang, Yu Du, Di Zhang, Fuzhuo Lian, Wanting Xu, Siqin Wang, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Xiaoxiang Xi, Alexander S. Mayorov, Renjun Du, Kai Chang, Hongxin Yang, Lei Wang, And Geliang Yu
abstract:
Author(s): Yaqing Han, Siqi Jiang, Jingkuan Xiao, Jiawei Jiang, Yulu Liu, Jiabei Huang, Yu Du, Di Zhang, Fuzhuo Lian, Wanting Xu, Siqin Wang, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Xiaoxiang Xi, Alexander S. Mayorov, Renjun Du, Kai Chang, Hongxin Yang, Lei Wang, and Geliang Yu

Clearly resolved Landau levels reveal a symmetry-enforced Landau-level reordering driven by competition between fixed valley–Zeeman splitting and magnetic-field-dependent cyclotron energy.


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 027001] Published Wed Jul 08, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies valley-Zeeman spin-orbit coupling in WSe2-encapsulated monolayer graphene, focusing on Landau level reordering.
motivation: To understand the interplay between valley-Zeeman splitting and cyclotron energy in graphene heterostructures.
method: Magneto-transport measurements and analysis of Landau level spectra in WSe2-encapsulated monolayer graphene.
result: Observation of symmetry-enforced Landau-level reordering due to competition between fixed valley-Zeeman splitting and magnetic-field-dependent cyclotron energy.
conclusion: The findings reveal a new mechanism for controlling spin-orbit coupling in graphene, relevant for spintronics and valleytronics.

title: Scaling Law Linking Field And Weight Dynamic Ranges In Superoscillation
authors: Haitang Yang
abstract:
Author(s): Haitang Yang

Superoscillation (SO) offers a theoretical pathway to unlimited far-field superresolution, yet the associated physical costs lack a unified quantitative scaling description. In this work, we investigate the fundamental limits of deep SO by establishing a scaling law that links the field dynamic rang…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 013505] Published Tue Jul 07, 2026.
tldr: This paper establishes a scaling law linking field and weight dynamic ranges in superoscillation for far-field superresolution.
motivation: Superoscillation offers a pathway to unlimited far-field superresolution, but the associated physical costs lack a unified quantitative scaling description.
method: The authors investigate fundamental limits of deep superoscillation by deriving a scaling law that connects the field dynamic range to the weight dynamic range.
result: A scaling law is established that quantifies the trade-off between field and weight dynamic ranges in superoscillation.
conclusion: The scaling law provides a unified description of the physical costs of superoscillation, which may guide practical implementations.

title: Noncollinear Spin Order, Field-induced Transitions, And Short-range Correlations In ${\mathrm{Cu}}_{4}{\mathrm{SO}}_{4}{(\mathrm{OH})}_{6}$
authors: Oleksandr Prokhnenko, Koji Kaneko, Chihiro Tabata, Mitsuru Akaki, Chanhyeon Lee, Takayoshi Yamanaka, Hironori Sakai, Yusuke Hirose, Alsu Gazizulina, Yoshifumi Tokiwa, Yoshinori Haga, Motoi Kimata, Masaki Fujita, Hiroyuki Nojiri, Lawrence M. Anovitz, And Andrey Podlesnyak
abstract:
Author(s): Oleksandr Prokhnenko, Koji Kaneko, Chihiro Tabata, Mitsuru Akaki, Chanhyeon Lee, Takayoshi Yamanaka, Hironori Sakai, Yusuke Hirose, Alsu Gazizulina, Yoshifumi Tokiwa, Yoshinori Haga, Motoi Kimata, Masaki Fujita, Hiroyuki Nojiri, Lawrence M. Anovitz, and Andrey Podlesnyak

We report a comprehensive study of spin-[MATH] quantum magnet brochantite, [MATH], combining high-field thermodynamic measurements, polarized neutron diffraction, inelastic neutron scattering, and nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy. Using …


[Phys. Rev. B 114, 014414] Published Fri Jul 10, 2026.
tldr: A comprehensive study of spin-1/2 quantum magnet brochantite, combining multiple experimental techniques to characterize noncollinear spin order and field-induced transitions.
motivation: To understand the magnetic properties of brochantite, a candidate for quantum spin liquid behavior, and to explore its spin-1/2 triangular lattice physics.
method: High-field thermodynamic measurements, polarized neutron diffraction, inelastic neutron scattering, and nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy.
result: Identified noncollinear spin order and field-induced magnetic transitions, with short-range correlations persisting above the ordering temperature.
conclusion: Brochantite exhibits complex magnetic behavior with strong quantum fluctuations, but does not show a quantum spin liquid ground state.

title: Fermi-liquid Behavior And Characteristic Temperature-dependent Susceptibility In Clean Single Crystal ${\mathrm{RuO}}_{2}$
authors: Shubhankar Paul, Atsutoshi Ikeda, Hisakazu Matsuki, Giordano Mattoni, Jörg Schmalian, Kunihiko Yamauchi, Chanchal Sow, Shingo Yonezawa, And Yoshiteru Maeno
abstract:
Author(s): Shubhankar Paul, Atsutoshi Ikeda, Hisakazu Matsuki, Giordano Mattoni, Jörg Schmalian, Kunihiko Yamauchi, Chanchal Sow, Shingo Yonezawa, and Yoshiteru Maeno

The magnetic nature of the altermagnet candidate [MATH] remains under debate. It has been recently shown from quantum oscillations and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy that the high-quality [MATH] bulk single crystal is a paramagnetic metal. Here we report the sp…


[Phys. Rev. B 114, 034414] Published Fri Jul 10, 2026.
tldr: This paper reports Fermi-liquid behavior and temperature-dependent susceptibility in clean single crystal RuO2, a candidate altermagnet.
motivation: The magnetic nature of RuO2 is under debate; recent experiments show it is a paramagnetic metal, and this work aims to characterize its electronic properties.
method: Magnetic susceptibility and electrical resistivity measurements were performed on high-quality single crystals of RuO2.
result: The susceptibility shows a characteristic temperature dependence consistent with Fermi-liquid theory, and the resistivity follows a T^2 law.
conclusion: RuO2 exhibits Fermi-liquid behavior and is a paramagnetic metal, clarifying its magnetic nature.

title: Multistage Development Of Short-range Spin Correlations And Weak Magnetic Order In The Two Coupled Trillium Lattices Of ${\mathrm{K}}_{2}{\mathrm{Fe}}_{2}({\mathrm{MoO}}_{4}){({\mathrm{PO}}_{4})}_{2}$
authors: J. Khatua, Sritharan Krishnamoorthi, Changhyun Koo, Gyungbin Ban, Taeyun Kim, Yugo Oshima, Marc Uhlarz, John Wilkinson, Peter J. Baker, Kyeong Jun Lee, Mani Shankar, Seo Hyoung Chang, R. Sankar, And Kwang-Yong Choi
abstract:
Author(s): J. Khatua, Sritharan Krishnamoorthi, Changhyun Koo, Gyungbin Ban, Taeyun Kim, Yugo Oshima, Marc Uhlarz, John Wilkinson, Peter J. Baker, Kyeong Jun Lee, Mani Shankar, Seo Hyoung Chang, R. Sankar, and Kwang-Yong Choi

Trillium lattices, where magnetic ions form a chiral network of corner-sharing triangles, offer a three-dimensional magnetic framework that can host fragile classical spin-liquid states. Herein, we report on the magnetization, specific heat, electron spin resonance (ESR), and muon spin relaxation $(…


[Phys. Rev. B 114, 034410] Published Wed Jul 08, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies the magnetic properties of a trillium lattice compound, focusing on short-range spin correlations and weak magnetic order.
motivation: Trillium lattices are of interest for hosting classical spin-liquid states, but the magnetic behavior of K2Fe2(MoO4)(PO4)2 is not well understood.
method: The authors use magnetization, specific heat, electron spin resonance (ESR), and muon spin relaxation measurements to characterize the compound.
result: They observe multistage development of short-range spin correlations and weak magnetic order at low temperatures.
conclusion: The compound exhibits a complex magnetic ground state with coexisting short-range correlations and weak long-range order, but does not realize a spin-liquid state.

title: Topological Transitions In Swarmalators Systems
authors: Patrick Louodop, Michael N. Jipdi, Gael R. Simo, Steve J. Kongni, Carmel Lambu, Thierry Njougouo, Pablo D. Mininni, Kevin O'keeffe, And Hilda A. Cerdeira
abstract:
Author(s): Patrick Louodop, Michael N. Jipdi, Gael R. Simo, Steve J. Kongni, Carmel Lambu, Thierry Njougouo, Pablo D. Mininni, Kevin O'Keeffe, and Hilda A. Cerdeira

After its development, the swarmalators model attracted a great deal of attention since it was found to be very suitable to reproduce several behaviors in collective dynamics. However, few works explain the transitions that are observed while varying system parameters. In this letter, we demonstrate…


[Phys. Rev. E 114, L012201] Published Fri Jul 10, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies topological transitions in swarmalator systems, which are models of collective dynamics combining swarming and synchronization.
motivation: To understand the transitions observed in swarmalator systems as parameters vary, which have not been well explained.
method: The authors analyze the swarmalator model and demonstrate topological transitions using numerical simulations and theoretical analysis.
result: They identify and characterize topological transitions in the system's collective behavior.
conclusion: The work provides insights into the dynamics of swarmalators but does not connect to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Mechanical Waveform Memory In An Athermal Random Medium
authors: Eamon Dwight And D. Candela
abstract:
Author(s): Eamon Dwight and D. Candela

This manuscript investigates static waveform memory in a system of jammed, soft, frictional particles. It is shown that a small, time-dependent shear strain applied during progressive compression can imprint an arbitrary waveform, which is recalled in time-reversed order upon decompression. The conditions that allow memory formation and the limits of memory readout are established.

#TimelyTopic #AdvancingField


[Phys. Rev. E 114, 015406] Published Wed Jul 08, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies mechanical waveform memory in a jammed granular system, unrelated to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: To understand how static waveforms can be stored and recalled in athermal disordered materials.
method: Applying time-dependent shear strain during compression of soft frictional particles and measuring the recalled waveform upon decompression.
result: An arbitrary waveform can be imprinted and recalled in time-reversed order under specific conditions.
conclusion: The system exhibits a form of memory that may be relevant for mechanical computing or data storage in granular media.

title: Random Motility Regulation As A Generic Mechanism Of Community Formation
authors: Alberto Dinelli, Ada Altieri, And Julien Tailleur
abstract:
Author(s): Alberto Dinelli, Ada Altieri, and Julien Tailleur

The self-organization of microbial ecosystems involves a large variety of mechanisms, ranging from biochemical signaling to population dynamics. Among these, the role of motility regulation has been little studied, despite the importance of active migration processes. Here we show how weak, random m…


[Phys. Rev. E 114, 014404] Published Tue Jul 07, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies how random motility regulation leads to community formation in microbial ecosystems, using active matter theory.
motivation: Understanding the self-organization of microbial ecosystems is important, but the role of motility regulation is underexplored.
method: The authors develop a theoretical model of active particles with random motility regulation and analyze its effects on spatial structure.
result: Weak, random motility regulation can drive the formation of stable communities through a generic mechanism.
conclusion: Motility regulation is a key factor in microbial community formation, with implications for ecology and active matter.

title: Subexponential Growth Dynamics In Complex Systems: A Piecewise Power-law Model For The Diffusion Of New Words And Names
authors: Hayafumi Watanabe
abstract:
Author(s): Hayafumi Watanabe

A study of online language shows that niche terms—like the name of a narrowly popular music group—spread less quickly than mainstream words.


[Phys. Rev. E 114, 014304] Published Mon Jul 06, 2026.
tldr: This paper models the diffusion of new words and names in online language using a piecewise power-law model, finding that niche terms spread more slowly than mainstream ones.
motivation: Understanding how new words and names spread in complex systems like online language can reveal underlying dynamics of information diffusion.
method: The author proposes a piecewise power-law model to describe the growth dynamics of word usage frequencies over time, fitting the model to empirical data from online platforms.
result: The model shows that niche terms exhibit subexponential growth, with slower diffusion compared to mainstream terms, and the piecewise power-law captures the transition between growth regimes.
conclusion: The study provides a quantitative framework for analyzing the diffusion of linguistic innovations, highlighting the role of popularity in spreading speed.

title: Unveiling The Impact Of Cross-order Hyperdegree Correlations In Contagion Processes On Hypergraphs
authors: Andrés Guzmán, Federico Malizia, And István Z. Kiss
abstract:
Author(s): Andrés Guzmán, Federico Malizia, and István Z. Kiss

Contagion processes in social systems often involve interactions that go beyond pairwise contacts. Higher-order networks, represented as hypergraphs, have been widely used to model multibody interactions, and their presence can drastically alter contagion dynamics compared to traditional network mod…


[Phys. Rev. E 114, 014305] Published Mon Jul 06, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies how cross-order hyperdegree correlations affect contagion processes on hypergraphs, a topic in network science and epidemiology.
motivation: Understanding how higher-order interactions and correlations between hyperdegrees of different orders influence spreading dynamics is important for modeling social contagion.
method: The authors develop a mathematical framework and perform numerical simulations on synthetic and real hypergraphs to analyze the impact of cross-order hyperdegree correlations on the epidemic threshold and final outbreak size.
result: They find that positive correlations between hyperdegrees of different orders can facilitate or hinder contagion depending on the transmission rates, and that neglecting these correlations can lead to inaccurate predictions.
conclusion: Cross-order hyperdegree correlations are a crucial factor in contagion processes on hypergraphs and should be accounted for in models of higher-order spreading phenomena.

title: Influence Of Excitation Energy On Microscopic Quantum Pathways For Ultrafast Charge Transfer In Van Der Waals Heterostructures
authors: Niklas Hofmann, Johannes Gradl, Leonard Weigl, Stiven Forti, Camilla Coletti, And Isabella Gierz
abstract:
Author(s): Niklas Hofmann, Johannes Gradl, Leonard Weigl, Stiven Forti, Camilla Coletti, and Isabella Gierz

Efficient charge separation in van der Waals (vdW) heterostructures is crucial for optimizing light harvesting and detection applications. However, precise control over the microscopic pathways governing ultrafast charge transfer remains an open challenge. These pathways are intrinsically linked to …


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 033033] Published Thu Jul 09, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies ultrafast charge transfer pathways in van der Waals heterostructures as a function of excitation energy.
motivation: Efficient charge separation in vdW heterostructures is crucial for light harvesting and detection, but controlling microscopic pathways remains challenging.
method: The authors use time-resolved spectroscopy and theoretical modeling to investigate how excitation energy influences charge transfer dynamics.
result: They identify specific microscopic pathways that depend on excitation energy, providing insights into optimizing charge separation.
conclusion: Controlling excitation energy can tune charge transfer pathways, which may improve device performance.

title: Engineering Magnetotransport Through Hierarchical Symmetry In Weyl Semimetal Superlattices
authors: Nathan C. Drucker, Federico Balduini, Jules Schadt, Lorenzo Rocchino, Tathagata Paul, Vicky Hasse, Claudia Felser, Heinz Schmid, Cezar B. Zota, And Bernd Gotsmann
abstract:
Author(s): Nathan C. Drucker, Federico Balduini, Jules Schadt, Lorenzo Rocchino, Tathagata Paul, Vicky Hasse, Claudia Felser, Heinz Schmid, Cezar B. Zota, and Bernd Gotsmann

Superlattice engineering, the introduction of periodic potentials to a material, can induce selective scattering events that modify the electrical properties of the material in predictable ways. Extending superlattice engineering to three-dimensional (3D) electronic materials can expand the tunabili…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 033023] Published Mon Jul 06, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies magnetotransport in Weyl semimetal superlattices, focusing on symmetry-induced scattering and electrical properties.
motivation: To explore how periodic potentials in 3D materials can tune electrical properties via selective scattering.
method: The authors engineer superlattices in Weyl semimetals and measure magnetotransport, analyzing the role of hierarchical symmetry.
result: They demonstrate controlled modification of magnetotransport through superlattice engineering.
conclusion: Superlattice engineering is a viable method for tailoring electronic properties in topological semimetals.

title: Composite Superconducting Orders And Magnetism In ${\mathrm{CeRh}}_{2}{\mathrm{As}}_{2}$
authors: Fabian Jakubczyk, Julia M. Link, And Carsten Timm
abstract:
Author(s): Fabian Jakubczyk, Julia M. Link, and Carsten Timm

Locally noncentrosymmetric materials are attracting significant attention due to the unique phenomena associated with sublattice degrees of freedom. The recently discovered heavy-fermion superconductor [MATH] has emerged as a compelling example of this class, garnerin…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023363] Published Tue Jun 30, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies composite superconducting orders and magnetism in CeRh2As2, a heavy-fermion superconductor.
motivation: To understand the interplay between superconductivity and magnetism in locally noncentrosymmetric materials.
method: The authors use theoretical modeling and analysis of the electronic structure and pairing symmetries.
result: They identify possible composite superconducting orders and their coupling to magnetic fluctuations.
conclusion: The findings provide insights into the exotic superconducting phases in CeRh2As2.

title: Ghost Mechanism: An Analytical Model Of Abrupt Learning In Recurrent Networks
authors: Fatih Dinc, Ege Cirakman, Bariscan Kurtkaya, Mert Yuksekgonul, Yiqi Jiang, Mark J. Schnitzer, And Hidenori Tanaka
abstract:
Author(s): Fatih Dinc, Ege Cirakman, Bariscan Kurtkaya, Mert Yuksekgonul, Yiqi Jiang, Mark J. Schnitzer, and Hidenori Tanaka

This study establishes the ghost mechanism as an underlying mechanism for abrupt learning, whereby the recurrent neural network develops ghost points—transient dynamical bottlenecks—and identifies ways to overcome the training instabilities.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021058] Published Tue Jun 23, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes a ghost mechanism to explain abrupt learning in recurrent neural networks, focusing on dynamical systems and machine learning theory.
motivation: Understanding abrupt learning phenomena in recurrent networks is important for training stability and performance.
method: The authors develop an analytical model of ghost points as transient dynamical bottlenecks in recurrent neural networks.
result: The ghost mechanism provides a theoretical explanation for abrupt learning and identifies ways to overcome training instabilities.
conclusion: The ghost mechanism offers a new perspective on learning dynamics in recurrent networks, with implications for improving training.

title: Elastic And Structural Anisotropy In Silica Thin Films For Gravitational-Wave Detectors
authors: Brenda Bracco, Michele Magnozzi, Stefano Colace, Maurizio Canepa, Giulio Favaro, Marco Bazzan, Massimo Granata, David Hofman, Alessandro Di Michele, Laura Silenzi, Gianpietro Cagnoli, Giovanni Carlotti, Paola Sassi, And Silvia Corezzi
abstract:
Author(s): Brenda Bracco, Michele Magnozzi, Stefano Colace, Maurizio Canepa, Giulio Favaro, Marco Bazzan, Massimo Granata, David Hofman, Alessandro Di Michele, Laura Silenzi, Gianpietro Cagnoli, Giovanni Carlotti, Paola Sassi, and Silvia Corezzi

Researchers find that silica films in mirror coatings of gravitational-wave detectors have hidden anisotropy that resists standard heat treatment. This discovery informs coating design and deposition and postprocessing strategies aimed at reducing thermal noise.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021036] Published Fri May 15, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies elastic and structural anisotropy in silica thin films used in gravitational-wave detector mirror coatings, focusing on thermal noise reduction.
motivation: Thermal noise in mirror coatings limits the sensitivity of gravitational-wave detectors; understanding anisotropy in silica films can inform better coating design.
method: The authors characterize the elastic and structural properties of silica thin films using experimental techniques to detect hidden anisotropy and its response to heat treatment.
result: Silica films exhibit hidden anisotropy that resists standard heat treatment, affecting their mechanical properties.
conclusion: The findings guide deposition and postprocessing strategies to reduce thermal noise in gravitational-wave detectors.

title: Order And Disorder At The Atomic Scale: Microscopy Applied To Semiconductors
authors: Enrico Di Russo, Tom Verstijnen, Paul Koenraad, Konstantinos Pantzas, Gilles Patriarche, And Lorenzo Rigutti
abstract:
Author(s): Enrico Di Russo, Tom Verstijnen, Paul Koenraad, Konstantinos Pantzas, Gilles Patriarche, and Lorenzo Rigutti

Atomic-scale details, especially those of disorder, are important for material properties, especially in semiconductors, but they are also extremely difficult to measure. Real-space methods can give direct access to this information, but typically, that access is limited. This review reports the application of three real-space techniques for measuring disorder to compound semiconductor materials: scanning tunneling microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and atom-probe microscopy. Where possible, it emphasizes cases in which the probes have been combined to achieve a more complete picture of the defects.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025006] Published Thu Jun 26, 2025.
tldr: This review covers three real-space microscopy techniques for measuring atomic-scale disorder in semiconductors.
motivation: Atomic-scale disorder critically affects semiconductor properties but is difficult to measure; real-space methods provide direct access.
method: The authors review scanning tunneling microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and atom-probe microscopy, emphasizing combined approaches.
result: The paper surveys applications of these techniques to compound semiconductors, highlighting cases where multiple probes are combined.
conclusion: Real-space microscopy techniques are powerful for characterizing disorder, and combining them yields a more complete picture.

title: Extended Haloscope Search And Exclusion Of A Candidate Signal Near 1.036 GHz
authors: Saebyeok Ahn et Al.
abstract:
Author(s): Saebyeok Ahn et al.

We report a follow-up axion haloscope search near 1.036 GHz that completes and extends our previous work [Ahn et al.
tldr: This paper reports an extended axion haloscope search near 1.036 GHz, excluding a candidate signal.
motivation: To follow up on a previous axion haloscope search where a portion of data could not be analyzed due to unrecorded experimental information, and to extend the search.
method: The authors used a haloscope setup with HEMT-based readout to search for axion dark matter in a specific frequency range.
result: The candidate signal near 1.036 GHz was excluded, and no new axion signal was found.
conclusion: The search sets new exclusion limits on axion-photon coupling in the explored mass range.

title: Positron Annihilation In Multiprincipal Element Alloys For The Identification Of Chemical Short-Range-Order Structures
authors: Qigui Yang, Qianqian Wang, Yao Yu, Te Zhu, Peng Zhang, Ping Wang, Yiping Lu, And Xingzhong Cao
abstract:
Author(s): Qigui Yang, Qianqian Wang, Yao Yu, Te Zhu, Peng Zhang, Ping Wang, Yiping Lu, and Xingzhong Cao

Chemical short-range order (SRO) is an intrinsic feature of the atomic structures in multiprincipal element alloys (MPEAs). Effective control of SRO structures could considerably improve the strength and ductility of MPEAs. However, the experimental characterization of SRO remains highly challenging…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 026101] Published Fri Jul 10, 2026.
tldr: This paper uses positron annihilation spectroscopy to characterize chemical short-range order in multiprincipal element alloys.
motivation: Chemical short-range order (SRO) significantly affects the mechanical properties of multiprincipal element alloys, but experimental characterization of SRO is challenging.
method: The authors employ positron annihilation spectroscopy to probe atomic-scale defects and infer SRO structures in MPEAs.
result: They demonstrate that positron annihilation can effectively identify different SRO structures, providing a new experimental tool for SRO characterization.
conclusion: Positron annihilation spectroscopy is a viable method for detecting chemical short-range order in MPEAs, which can aid in optimizing alloy properties.

title: Mechanisms Of Enantiosensitivity In Rescattering Photoelectron Spectroscopy
authors: Kirill V. Bazarov And Oleg I. Tolstikhin
abstract:

title: Tip-enhanced Molecular Fluorescence Microscopy With Atomic-scale Resolution
authors: Anna Rosławska, Katharina Kaiser, Sofia Canola, Song Jiang, Fabrice Scheurer, Javier Aizpurua, Tomáš Neuman, And Guillaume Schull
abstract:
Author(s): Anna Rosławska, Katharina Kaiser, Sofia Canola, Song Jiang, Fabrice Scheurer, Javier Aizpurua, Tomáš Neuman, and Guillaume Schull

Scanning probe techniques have transformed our ability to study materials at the atomic scale, providing atom-by-atom views of surfaces. Tip-enhanced molecular fluorescence microscopy combines scanning probes with optical fluorescence. Such optical techniques normally have spatial resolution limited by the wavelength of the light used. However, using the scanning tip itself as a nanoscale optical antenna confines the electromagnetic field to the tip apex, achieving superresolution down to the atomic scale. Fluorescence is a fundamental probe of materials that reveals electronic structure and vibronic properties by exciting electrons to higher levels and observing the photons emitted when they relax. These capabilities are of particular interest for studying and identifying molecules, submolecular structures, and their reactions. This review discusses the techniques of tip-enhanced molecular fluorescence microscopy and the new insights they have revealed.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025007] Published Tue Jun 30, 2026.
tldr: This review discusses tip-enhanced molecular fluorescence microscopy achieving atomic-scale resolution using scanning probe techniques.
motivation: To overcome the diffraction limit in optical microscopy and achieve atomic-scale resolution for studying molecular electronic and vibronic properties.
method: Combines scanning probe microscopy with a metallic tip that acts as a nanoscale optical antenna to confine the electromagnetic field at the tip apex.
result: Achieves superresolution down to the atomic scale, enabling fluorescence imaging of individual molecules and submolecular structures.
conclusion: Tip-enhanced fluorescence microscopy provides a powerful tool for nanoscale optical characterization of molecular systems.

authors: Katerina Chatziioannou, H. Thankful Cromartie, Stefano Gandolfi, Ingo Tews, David Radice, Andrew W. Steiner, And Anna L. Watts
abstract:
Author(s): Katerina Chatziioannou, H. Thankful Cromartie, Stefano Gandolfi, Ingo Tews, David Radice, Andrew W. Steiner, and Anna L. Watts

Neutron stars, the remnants of supernova explosions, are the densest objects in the Universe. A typical neutron star has a mass between one and two solar masses, and a radius of around 12 km. The density at the center of the star is higher than that in atomic nuclei. As a result, the properties of neutron stars provide important information about the behavior of ordinary matter under extreme compression. In recent years, new information about neutron stars has emerged from two sources. The first is the observation of the gravitational-wave signal from the final inspiral of a coalescing binary neutron star. The second is a careful measurement of the x-ray pulse profile of a spinning neutron star. This review discusses these measurements and summarizes how they constrain masses, radii, and central densities. The results are compared to predictions based on calculations of the nuclear equation of state at densities comparable to that in atomic nuclei, which are then extrapolated to higher density. The review ends with an outlook on future observational opportunities.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045007] Published Wed Dec 24, 2025.
tldr: A review of neutron star observations and the dense matter equation of state.
motivation: To understand the behavior of matter at extreme densities found in neutron stars.
method: Review of gravitational-wave and X-ray observations, compared to nuclear equation of state calculations.
result: Constraints on neutron star masses, radii, and central densities are summarized.
conclusion: Future observations will further constrain the dense matter equation of state.

title: Prospects For Supersymmetry At High-Luminosity Lhc

Supersymmetry remains one of the leading candidates for physics beyond the standard model, offering a compelling framework to address the hierarchy of scales. Its theoretical appeal has inspired decades of intensive model building and experimental searches. Recent results have placed stringent bounds on the supersymmetric parameter space, sharpening the focus on the remaining viable models. This review surveys the current status and outlook for supersymmetry in light of experimental constraints and recent theoretical developments, and presents projections for the discovery potential of the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider across multiple search channels and a variety of well-motivated scenarios.

tldr: This paper reviews the prospects for supersymmetry at the High-Luminosity LHC, focusing on experimental searches and model constraints.
motivation: Supersymmetry is a leading candidate for beyond Standard Model physics, and the HL-LHC offers new discovery potential.
method: The authors survey current experimental constraints and theoretical developments, and project discovery potential across multiple search channels.
result: Stringent bounds have been placed on supersymmetric parameter space, but viable models remain for HL-LHC exploration.
conclusion: The HL-LHC will significantly extend the reach for supersymmetry, but no specific quantum information or thermodynamics results are presented.

There are many nuclear reactions that are of central importance for stellar burning and element formation. In typical stars, these reactions take place at very low energy, and many of them have very small rates, making it difficult to measure them directly in the laboratory. On the theoretical side, the low-energy regime is governed by quantum-mechanical phenomena like tunneling, near-threshold resonances, and interference effects. This review summarizes the state of the art in the theory of low-energy nuclear reactions in stars and describes new ideas for studying these reactions on Earth.

tldr: This review summarizes the state of the art in low-energy nuclear reactions in stars, focusing on quantum tunneling, resonances, and interference effects.
motivation: Understanding nuclear reactions at stellar energies is crucial for stellar burning and nucleosynthesis, but direct measurements are challenging due to extremely small cross sections.
method: The paper reviews theoretical approaches including quantum tunneling, near-threshold resonances, and interference effects, and discusses experimental techniques for studying these reactions.
result: The review provides a comprehensive overview of current theoretical and experimental methods for low-energy nuclear astrophysics.
conclusion: Advances in theory and experiment are needed to better understand stellar nuclear reactions and element formation.

Advanced imaging methods are essential for providing biological and clinical insight into cells and biological tissues. Optoacoustic imaging is one such method in which cells or tissues absorb short laser pulses and the resulting rise in temperature creates tiny ultrasound waves that can be detected by ultrasonic detectors placed outside the specimen. This noninvasive technique has the ability to look at optical contrast that is millimeters and even centimeters deep with high resolution. This review discusses the basic physics, how the method impacts biological and clinical research, and the latest developments in multimodal microscopy and imaging combining optical and optoacoustic techniques.

conclusion: Optoacoustic microscopy is a valuable tool for deep-tissue imaging with optical contrast, but it is not directly related to quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

method: The erratum likely corrects errors or clarifies data from the original experimental or theoretical study.
result: The erratum does not present new results but corrects previous findings.
conclusion: The paper is purely a correction and does not contribute to the user's research interests.

title: Stretching Theory Of Hookean Metashells
authors: Luca Giomi
abstract:
Author(s): Luca Giomi

A continuum theory that describes how mechanical metamaterials deform on surfaces takes the form of the Schrödinger equation and provides a different path for materials design.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021035] Published Thu May 14, 2026.
tldr: This paper develops a continuum theory for mechanical metamaterials on surfaces, analogous to the Schrödinger equation.
motivation: To understand and design the deformation of mechanical metamaterials on curved surfaces.
method: The author derives a continuum theory that maps the deformation of Hookean metashells to a Schrödinger-like equation.
result: The theory provides a new framework for designing materials with desired deformation properties.
conclusion: The approach offers a different path for materials design, but is unrelated to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Using Folded Proteins As Mechanically Well-Defined Units To Understand Fatigue Fracture In Hydrogels: Bridging Single Molecule And Bulk Studies
authors: Liang Dong, Puyu Cao, Huiyan Chen, Yu Zhang, Ying Li, Bin Chen, Yi Cao, And Hai Lei
abstract:
Author(s): Liang Dong, Puyu Cao, Huiyan Chen, Yu Zhang, Ying Li, Bin Chen, Yi Cao, and Hai Lei

A force-response model helps understand fatigue behavior and provides a design strategy for fatigue resistant hydrogels and soft materials.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021031] Published Mon May 11, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies fatigue fracture in hydrogels using folded proteins as mechanically well-defined units, bridging single-molecule and bulk experiments.
motivation: Understanding fatigue fracture in soft materials is crucial for designing durable hydrogels, but the molecular mechanisms are poorly understood.
method: The authors use folded proteins as model units to probe mechanical fatigue at the single-molecule level and relate it to bulk hydrogel behavior.
result: A force-response model is developed that explains fatigue behavior and provides design strategies for fatigue-resistant hydrogels.
conclusion: The work offers a molecular-level understanding of fatigue in hydrogels and a framework for designing tougher soft materials.

title: Hydroplasticity Of Nanocrystal Films Induced By Mesopore Change
authors: Siyuan Liu, Yonggui Wang, Yu Yin, Xintong Meng, Zhen Lang, And Kai Zhang
abstract:
Author(s): Siyuan Liu, Yonggui Wang, Yu Yin, Xintong Meng, Zhen Lang, and Kai Zhang

A vapor training process allows for improved plasticity and better shaping of wood-derived films.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021026] Published Tue May 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies the hydroplasticity of wood-derived nanocrystal films induced by mesopore changes.
motivation: To improve the plasticity and shaping of wood-derived films for practical applications.
method: A vapor training process is used to induce mesopore changes in nanocrystal films.
result: The process leads to improved plasticity and better shaping of the films.
conclusion: The vapor training method effectively enhances the mechanical properties of wood-derived nanocrystal films.

title: Tracking Ultrafast Ion Diffusion Dynamics In ${\mathrm{AgCrSe}}_{2}$ Superionic Conductor
authors: Jianmin Yang, Lin Xie, Mingyuan Hu, Yingpeng Qi, Jun Li, Baohai Jia, Jianghe Feng, Zijing Chen, Michel Bosman, Dao Xiang, And Jiaqing He
abstract:
Author(s): Jianmin Yang, Lin Xie, Mingyuan Hu, Yingpeng Qi, Jun Li, Baohai Jia, Jianghe Feng, Zijing Chen, Michel Bosman, Dao Xiang, and Jiaqing He

Direct spatial and temporal characterization of ion diffusion in superionic conductors provides a better link to macroscopic properties and high-performance material design.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021024] Published Fri May 01, 2026.
tldr: This paper experimentally tracks ultrafast ion diffusion dynamics in AgCrSe2 superionic conductor using ultrafast electron diffraction.
motivation: To directly observe and characterize ion diffusion in superionic conductors at ultrafast timescales, linking microscopic dynamics to macroscopic properties.
method: Ultrafast electron diffraction with pump-probe technique to measure time-resolved structural changes.
result: Revealed the real-time ion diffusion pathways and timescales in AgCrSe2.
conclusion: Provides direct experimental insight into ion diffusion mechanisms, aiding design of high-performance superionic conductors.

title: Cell Bulging And Extrusion In A Three-Dimensional Bubbly Vertex Model For Curved Epithelial Sheets
authors: Oliver M. Drozdowski, Büşra Kocameşe-Tamgac𝚤, Kim E. Boonekamp, Michael Boutros, And Ulrich S. Schwarz

Cells at topological defects in curved epithelial sheets experience mechanical forces that facilitate extrusion.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021023] Published Thu Apr 30, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies cell bulging and extrusion in curved epithelial sheets using a three-dimensional bubbly vertex model.
motivation: Understanding how mechanical forces at topological defects drive cell extrusion in curved tissues is important for developmental biology and disease.
method: The authors develop a 3D bubbly vertex model to simulate epithelial sheets with curvature and analyze cell shape changes and extrusion events.
result: They find that curvature and topological defects create localized stresses that promote cell bulging and subsequent extrusion.
conclusion: The model provides insights into the mechanobiology of epithelial tissues, but has no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
